solution.concept_anchor: Pug-mark census discrediting trigger and methodology shift
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because students often associate the methodology shift with a general scientific critique rather than the specific Sariska tiger extinction scandal that exposed census fraud.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): general scientific dissatisfaction existed earlier but was not the immediate trigger for the post-2006 methodology overhaul.
Eliminate option (c): the Panna tiger extinction occurred after the methodology shift was already underway — it was a consequence, not the trigger.
Eliminate option (d): there was no international audit mandated by a multilateral body that forced the change — this is a plausible-fabrication distractor.

Confirm option (b): Sariska Tiger Reserve's complete tiger extinction (confirmed 2004–05), despite pug-mark census showing healthy numbers, directly exposed the method's unreliability and triggered the WPA 2006 amendment and methodology overhaul.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap here is an entity-swap between Sariska and Panna. Both reserves lost all their tigers, but Sariska was the first and the direct catalyst for the 2006 legislative and methodological changes. A student who knows both episodes but conflates their sequence will select Panna. The pug-mark census was not abandoned merely because scientists disliked it — it was abandoned because Sariska's field reality contradicted its numbers, making the scandal the precise trigger.
solution.final_explanation:
The All India Tiger Estimation historically relied on pug-mark identification, where field staff collected pugmark impressions and used them to count individual tigers. This method was thoroughly discredited not by academic critique alone but by a real-world scandal.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: General scientific criticism of pug-mark methodology had existed for years without producing policy change.
• Option (b) — Correct: The complete extinction of tigers in Sariska Tiger Reserve (Rajasthan), confirmed in 2004–05, exposed that the pug-mark census had been recording phantom tigers. This directly triggered the Wildlife Protection Act Amendment of 2006 and the adoption of camera-trap and occupancy-survey-based methodology.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Panna's tiger loss occurred after the methodology was already being reformed.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: No multilateral audit mandated this change; it was a domestic policy response.

Value Addition:
• The WPA 2006 amendment also established NTCA as a statutory body, directly as a governance response to Sariska.
• Post-2006 methodology integrates four phases: sign surveys, camera traps, prey estimation, and habitat assessment.
• Sariska subsequently received tigers from Ranthambore through India's first inter-reserve reintroduction programme.

solution.concept_anchor: NTCA statutory basis and de-notification power

statement_analysis.statement: The National Tiger Conservation Authority derives its statutory authority from a dedicated legislation titled the Tiger Conservation Act, 2006.
statement_analysis.reason: NTCA was established under the Wildlife Protection Act 1972, as amended in 2006 — it has no standalone act. The Wildlife (Protection) Amendment Act 2006 inserted Chapter IVB to create NTCA.

statement_analysis.statement: De-notification of a Tiger Reserve by the NTCA requires the concurrence of the concerned State Government and the National Board for Wildlife.
statement_analysis.reason: The concurrence required is of the State Government and the Central Government's approval through the process involving CWC (Chief Wildlife Warden), not the National Board for Wildlife — the NBWL's role is in approving projects within protected areas, not in Tiger Reserve de-notification specifically.

statement_analysis.statement: Project Tiger preceded the NTCA and functioned as a Centrally Sponsored Scheme before the NTCA gave it statutory backing.
statement_analysis.reason: Project Tiger was launched in 1973 as a Centrally Sponsored Scheme under administrative direction. The Wildlife Protection Act amendment in 2006 created NTCA and gave Project Tiger's framework a statutory basis.

solution.strong_distractor: b — A student who correctly identifies Statement 3 as true may also be misled into accepting Statement 2 as true because the NBWL does play a major role in wildlife governance, creating a plausible but incorrect association with Tiger Reserve de-notification.
elimination_logic: Eliminate Statement 1 immediately: NTCA has no standalone act — it was inserted into the Wildlife Protection Act 1972 via the 2006 amendment.

Scrutinise Statement 2: De-notification requires State Government concurrence, but the specific body cited (NBWL) is not the mandated concurring authority for this process — making Statement 2 incorrect.
Confirm Statement 3: Project Tiger's 1973 launch as a Centrally Sponsored Scheme predates NTCA's 2006 statutory creation — this is factually established.
With only Statement 3 correct, select option (c): 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Two traps operate here. First, 'Tiger Conservation Act 2006' in Statement 1 sounds authoritative — students who know '2006' is the key year but not the precise legislation will accept it. Second, Statement 2 names the NBWL, which is a real and prominent body in wildlife governance, making it feel right. The correct concurring authority in the de-notification process is the State Government, and the process flows through the State's Chief Wildlife Warden, not the NBWL specifically.
solution.final_explanation:
NTCA's legislative underpinning is frequently misattributed in examination preparation material. There is no standalone Tiger Conservation Act.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: NTCA was created by amending the Wildlife Protection Act 1972 — specifically through Chapter IVB inserted by the Wildlife (Protection) Amendment Act 2006. No separate legislation named 'Tiger Conservation Act' exists.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: While the NTCA exercises powers related to Tiger Reserves, de-notification of a reserve requires State Government concurrence under Section 38V. The NBWL's jurisdiction pertains primarily to approving projects within and around protected areas, not Tiger Reserve de-notification.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Project Tiger (1973) was purely a Centrally Sponsored Scheme under executive orders. The 2006 WPA amendment gave this framework statutory backing through NTCA.

Value Addition:
• NTCA's composition includes the Minister of Environment (Chairperson), Members of Parliament, and technical experts.
• WCCB (Wildlife Crime Control Bureau) is often confused with NTCA — WCCB handles wildlife crime enforcement and is a separate statutory body under WPA.
• A Tiger Reserve can be notified by State Government on NTCA's recommendation under Section 38V, but de-notification requires Central approval.

solution.concept_anchor: Project Tiger funding pattern and initial reserve count

statement_analysis.statement: Project Tiger was launched in 1973 with nine tiger reserves under the direct administrative control of the Central Government.
statement_analysis.reason: While the launch year (1973) and initial count (9 reserves) are correct, tiger reserves under Project Tiger are managed by State Governments — not under direct Central Government administrative control. The Centre provides funding and policy direction but states manage the reserves.

statement_analysis.statement: The funding pattern for Project Tiger follows a 60:40 Centre-State ratio for all states, including those in the northeastern region.
statement_analysis.reason: The 60:40 ratio applies to general states, but northeastern and hill states receive a more favourable 90:10 Centre-State funding ratio under the Centrally Sponsored Scheme structure.

statement_analysis.statement: All Tiger Reserves in India are notified under Project Tiger, but the day-to-day management responsibility rests with the respective State Forest Departments.
statement_analysis.reason: Tiger Reserves are legally declared under the WPA and managed by states — Project Tiger provides the policy and funding framework, but field management is a state responsibility.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students will likely identify Statement 1 as incorrect due to the 'direct Central control' element, but may accept Statement 2 as true because '60:40' is the widely remembered ratio without recalling the northeastern states' differential.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 contains a partial-truth trap: the year and reserve count are correct but 'direct Central administrative control' is false — management is a state responsibility.
Statement 2 is incorrect: the 90:10 ratio for NE and hill states is a well-known special provision of Centrally Sponsored Schemes — the blanket '60:40 for all states' is wrong.
Statement 3 is correct: states manage Tiger Reserves under Project Tiger's framework — this is consistent with the federal structure.
Since Statements 1 and 2 are both NOT correct, option (b) — '1 and 2 only' — is the answer for the question asking which are NOT correct.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is the precision trap. The 60:40 Centre-State funding ratio is well known. The modification for northeastern and hill states (90:10) is a consistent feature of virtually all Centrally Sponsored Schemes, but students who haven't specifically linked this to Project Tiger's funding structure will mark Statement 2 as correct, selecting the wrong option.
solution.final_explanation:
Project Tiger (1973) operates as a Centrally Sponsored Scheme — one of the longest-running such schemes in India's conservation history.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The launch year (1973) and initial reserve count (9) are accurate, but the characterisation of 'direct Central administrative control' is wrong. Tiger Reserves are managed by State Forest Departments; the Centre provides funds and sets standards.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: For most states, the funding ratio under Project Tiger is 60:40 (Centre:State). However, northeastern states and hill states receive a 90:10 Centre-State ratio, reflecting the special category status of these regions under Centrally Sponsored Schemes.
• Statement 3 — Correct: All Tiger Reserves fall under Project Tiger's policy umbrella, but operational management is entirely with state governments through their Forest Departments.

Value Addition:
• India now has 55+ Tiger Reserves spanning over 75,000 sq km.
• The 2006 WPA amendment elevated Project Tiger from an administrative scheme to a statutory framework under NTCA.
• Project Tiger ≠ Tiger Reserves: The former is the scheme; the latter are the specific notified areas.

solution.concept_anchor: Buffer zone legal status under WPA — not necessarily a Protected Area
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know both facts tend to assume that because buffer zones are part of Tiger Reserves, they must automatically be Protected Areas under WPA, leading them to accept R as the correct explanation for A.
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is Assertion (A) correct? A states that human activities are permitted in the buffer zone of a Tiger Reserve to allow co-existence. This is factually correct — the buffer zone is designed for co-existence and compatible land uses.

Step 2 — Is Reason (R) correct? R states that buffer zones are notified as Wildlife Sanctuaries under the Wildlife Protection Act 1972. This is factually incorrect — buffer zones of Tiger Reserves are not necessarily notified as Wildlife Sanctuaries or any other Protected Area category under WPA. They may include revenue land, community forests, or other non-PA land.
Step 3 — Since R is factually incorrect, the correct option is (c): A is correct but R is incorrect.
Final check confirms: correct_option = c.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap exploits the assumption that because the buffer zone is part of a formally declared Tiger Reserve, it must automatically enjoy Protected Area status under WPA. In reality, the buffer zone may include revenue lands, panchayat forests, and community lands that are NOT notified as Wildlife Sanctuaries or National Parks. The Tiger Reserve is a broader administrative unit under Section 38V, and its buffer component does not necessarily carry the legal attributes of a PA.
solution.final_explanation:
Tiger Reserves under Section 38V of the WPA 1972 must have a mandatory two-zone structure: the core/Critical Tiger Habitat (inviolate) and the buffer zone (co-existence allowed).

Assertion (A): The buffer zone of a Tiger Reserve permits human activities and co-existence uses — this is correct. Buffer zones are explicitly designed to accommodate compatible human land use while protecting the core.

Reason (R): R claims that buffer zones are notified as Wildlife Sanctuaries under WPA — this is incorrect. Buffer zones may include revenue lands, community forests, reserve forests, or other non-Protected Area categories. They do not automatically acquire the legal status of a Wildlife Sanctuary or National Park simply by being included in a Tiger Reserve's boundary.

Since A is correct and R is incorrect, the answer is (c).

Value Addition:
• Core zones must be kept inviolate — no human activity is permitted, not even bona fide use.
• Eco-Sensitive Zones (ESZ) are different from buffer zones: ESZ lies outside the Tiger Reserve boundary; buffer is inside.
• State Government notifies the Tiger Reserve on NTCA's recommendation — both zones are declared simultaneously.

solution.concept_anchor: 2022 tiger census state-wise rankings and Guinness record

statement_analysis.statement: As per the 2022 tiger estimation, India holds approximately 75% of the world's wild tiger population.
statement_analysis.reason: India's 2022 tiger count of 3,167 represents approximately 75% of the estimated global wild tiger population, a figure officially cited in the Status of Tigers 2022 report.

statement_analysis.statement: Karnataka recorded the highest tiger population among all Indian states in the 2022 census.
statement_analysis.reason: Madhya Pradesh reclaimed the top position in 2022 with 785 tigers, ahead of Karnataka (563) and Uttarakhand (560). Karnataka had held the top spot in 2018.

statement_analysis.statement: The 2022 tiger census was recognised as the largest tiger population survey ever conducted globally.
statement_analysis.reason: The 2022 All India Tiger Estimation received a Guinness World Record for being the world's largest camera-trap wildlife survey.

statement_analysis.statement: Uttarakhand reported more tigers than Karnataka in the 2022 census.
statement_analysis.reason: Karnataka recorded 563 tigers and Uttarakhand recorded 560 tigers in the 2022 estimation — Karnataka ranked second, just ahead of Uttarakhand which ranked third.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) 'Only three' tempts students who correctly identify Statements 1 and 3 as true and are unsure about Statement 4, not recalling the narrow Karnataka-Uttarakhand margin.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct: India's ~75% share of global wild tigers is a well-established, officially cited figure.
Statement 2 is incorrect: Karnataka topped the 2018 census; Madhya Pradesh reclaimed the lead in 2022 with 785 tigers.
Statement 3 is correct: the 2022 census received a Guinness World Record for the largest camera-trap wildlife survey.
Statement 4 is incorrect: Karnataka (563) ranked second, just above Uttarakhand (560) — Uttarakhand did NOT surpass Karnataka.
Only Statements 1 and 3 are correct → Only two → option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Two geographic-swap traps are embedded. First, Karnataka vs. Madhya Pradesh: Karnataka led in 2018 and students who memorised the 2018 rankings will select Karnataka as the top state. Second, the Karnataka vs. Uttarakhand margin (563 vs. 560) is so narrow that students who recall only that both are major tiger states will guess incorrectly. The Guinness Record detail (Statement 3) is genuine and tests awareness of the 2022 census's scale significance.
solution.final_explanation:
The 2022 Status of Tigers report (5th cycle of AITE) marked a significant milestone in India's conservation story.

• Statement 1 — Correct: With 3,167 tigers counted, India hosts ~75% of wild tigers globally — a figure officially cited by MoEFCC and NTCA.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Madhya Pradesh led the 2022 count with 785 tigers, reclaiming the top spot it had lost in 2018. Karnataka ranked second (563), not first.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The 2022 AITE covered over 600 protected areas across 20 states and received a Guinness World Record for the largest camera-trap wildlife survey ever conducted.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: Karnataka (563) narrowly edged out Uttarakhand (560). The margin is only 3 tigers, making this a precision knowledge test.

Only Statements 1 and 3 are correct → Only two → option (b).

Value Addition:
• 2018 tiger count was 2,967; 2022 count was 3,167 — approximately 6% growth over 4 years.
• MP–Karnataka–Uttarakhand is the top-3 order to memorise for 2022.
• The next estimation (6th cycle) is expected in 2026.

All India Tiger Estimation (AITE): Methodology Evolution

solution.concept_anchor: M-STrIPES function vs. camera trap methodology in tiger monitoring
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know M-STrIPES is a monitoring tool may conflate it with the periodic census (AITE), reversing the A–1 and B–2 pairings.
elimination_logic: M-STrIPES is a mobile-based patrolling and monitoring tool for continuous tiger surveillance — it is NOT the periodic census system; this anchors A to 3.
Camera trap grid methodology uses 25 sq km grid cells with double cameras to identify individual tigers via stripe patterns — this is the core of AITE's estimation phase; B pairs with 1.
Individual tiger identification through stripe patterns is the biological basis that makes camera-trap methodology work — C pairs with 4.
Line transect method is used for prey density estimation (ungulates) in AITE Phase I — D pairs with 2, confirming option (c): A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap lies in M-STrIPES (List I, item A): students who know it is related to tigers may conflate it with the periodic tiger estimation (AITE) and match it with item 1 (25 sq km camera grid). In reality, M-STrIPES is a continuous patrolling tool separate from the quadrennial estimation exercise. Similarly, conflating 'individual identification via stripe patterns' (C) with the camera grid methodology (B) is a common mistake because both involve cameras.
solution.final_explanation:
Tiger monitoring in India uses two distinct systems that must not be conflated: M-STrIPES for continuous patrolling-based monitoring, and the AITE camera-trap framework for periodic population estimation.

• A–3 (M-STrIPES: mobile-based patrolling tool): M-STrIPES enables forest guards to record patrol data, wildlife sightings, and violation alerts on mobile devices. It supports continuous monitoring between census cycles.
• B–1 (Camera trap grid: 25 sq km cells with double cameras): The AITE uses a standardised 25 sq km grid where two cameras are placed facing each other at the same point to capture both flanks of a tiger, enabling individual ID.
• C–4 (Individual ID via stripe patterns): No two tigers share identical stripe patterns — analogous to human fingerprints. This biological uniqueness is what makes camera-trap identification scientifically valid.
• D–2 (Line transect for prey density): Prey species (deer, wild boar, gaur) are counted using line transects. Tiger density is directly correlated with prey density — this is Phase I of AITE.

Value Addition:
• M-STrIPES data feeds into NTCA's real-time monitoring dashboard.
• The AITE also uses DNA-based fecal analysis to supplement camera-trap counts in dense vegetation.
• Prey estimation is as important as tiger counting — a reserve with declining prey is a conservation warning sign.

solution.concept_anchor: Tiger corridor legal protection gap under WPA

statement_analysis.statement: Tiger corridors in India lack specific legal protection under the Wildlife Protection Act 1972, as they generally fall outside the formally notified Protected Area network.
statement_analysis.reason: WPA 1972 provides legal protection to National Parks, Wildlife Sanctuaries, Conservation Reserves, and Community Reserves — but tiger corridors are not a recognised legal category under the Act and mostly traverse revenue lands, reserve forests, or private lands.

statement_analysis.statement: The Wildlife Institute of India has identified 32 functional tiger corridors nationally, including the Terai Arc Landscape, Central Indian Landscape, and Western Ghats Landscape as the three major tiger landscapes.
statement_analysis.reason: WII's corridor mapping has identified 32 functional corridors connecting tiger populations. The three named landscapes — Terai Arc, Central Indian, and Western Ghats — are the primary tiger landscapes in India where these corridors operate.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Students aware of the legal gap but uncertain about the specific number '32' may think Statement 2 is fabricated, selecting option (c) which marks only Statement 1 as correct.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Tiger corridors are not listed as a Protected Area category under WPA 1972 — they traverse revenue lands and non-PA areas; Statement 1 is correct.

Verify Statement 2: WII has indeed mapped 32 functional corridors across India's tiger landscapes; the three named landscapes (Terai Arc, Central Indian, Western Ghats) are officially recognised and frequently cited in conservation literature — Statement 2 is correct.
Both statements are independently correct → option (a) is the answer.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in Statement 1 lies in what students might expect: since Tiger Reserves are legally protected, many assume the corridors connecting them also enjoy legal protection. This is incorrect. Corridors are typically unprotected lands and receive no designated legal status under WPA. Statement 2's trap is the specific number '32' — students unfamiliar with this precise figure may dismiss it as fabricated.
solution.final_explanation:
Tiger corridors are critical for preventing genetic isolation of tiger sub-populations, yet they occupy a legal vacuum in India's conservation framework.

• Statement 1 — Correct: WPA 1972 recognises National Parks, Wildlife Sanctuaries, Conservation Reserves, and Community Reserves as Protected Areas. Tiger corridors are not a notified category — they traverse revenue lands, reserve forests (which have reduced protection), and even agricultural landscapes, leaving them vulnerable to development pressures.
• Statement 2 — Correct: WII's national corridor mapping exercise identified 32 functional corridors. The three major tiger landscapes — Terai Arc Landscape (sub-Himalayan belt), Central Indian Landscape (MP-Maharashtra heartland), and Western Ghats Landscape (south India) — together account for the majority of India's tiger population and corridor connectivity needs.

Both statements are correct → option (a).

Value Addition:
• Corridors face threats from highways, railways, linear infrastructure, and encroachment.
• The National Tiger Conservation Authority can issue advisories on corridor protection but cannot legally enforce them as Protected Areas.
• Some corridors are partly protected through Eco-Sensitive Zone notifications around Tiger Reserves.

solution.concept_anchor: WII institutional status — autonomous not statutory
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students aware that WII works closely with the Ministry of Environment and provides technical inputs to NTCA (a statutory body) often assume WII itself has statutory status.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): 'statutory body' implies creation by an Act of Parliament — WII was not created by any legislation and therefore does not qualify as a statutory body.
Eliminate option (b): 'constitutional body' requires establishment under a provision of the Constitution of India — WII has no constitutional basis.
Eliminate option (d): WII is not an independent regulatory authority; it is a research and training institution under MoEFCC.

Confirm option (c): WII is an autonomous institution established in 1982 under MoEFCC — it functions independently for research and technical purposes but draws its administrative shelter from the Ministry.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap works by proximity: WII provides technical inputs to NTCA, which IS a statutory body. Students who know WII's close working relationship with NTCA and the Ministry may assume WII shares NTCA's statutory character. In UPSC questions, the distinction between 'statutory body' (created by an Act), 'constitutional body' (created by the Constitution), and 'autonomous institution' (created by executive order/resolution under a Ministry) is a recurring precision test.
solution.final_explanation:
The Wildlife Institute of India (WII) is often confused with statutory conservation bodies due to its prominent role in tiger estimation.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: A statutory body is created by an Act of Parliament (e.g., NTCA under WPA 1972). WII was established by an executive resolution — it has no parliamentary statute creating it.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Constitutional bodies (e.g., UPSC, CAG) are established under specific constitutional articles. WII has no such basis.
• Option (c) — Correct: WII is an autonomous institution established in 1982 under the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change. 'Autonomous' here means it has its own governing council and operational independence, but it is not a statutory or constitutional body.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: WII is not a regulatory authority — it does not issue licences, enforce laws, or exercise quasi-judicial powers.

Value Addition:
• WII is headquartered in Dehradun, Uttarakhand.
• WII is the technical partner for AITE — it conducts surveys, analyses data, and publishes the Status of Tigers report.
• NTCA (policy/regulatory) + WII (science/technical) is the standard division of roles in tiger governance.

solution.concept_anchor: FRA 2006 vs. CTH — voluntary relocation requirement
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) sounds plausible because the inviolate status of core zones is a real and strong principle, leading students to think forced relocation is permissible for CTH protection.
elimination_logic: The scenario involves a tribal community with settled forest rights facing relocation from a Critical Tiger Habitat — the governing legal framework is Section 38V of WPA 1972 read with the Forest Rights Act 2006.
Eliminate option (b): Habeas corpus is a fundamental rights writ — it protects against illegal detention of a person, not displacement from land. This is a distractor.

Eliminate option (c): The inviolate status of CTH is a real principle, but it does NOT override the requirement that relocation from CTH must be voluntary with a rehabilitation package — forced eviction is legally prohibited even for CTH.
Eliminate option (d): CAMPA funds are for compensatory afforestation — they are not a legal basis for overriding community forest rights.

Confirm option (a): Under FRA 2006 and the WPA framework, relocation from CTH requires voluntary consent of the gram sabha, settlement of rights, and provision of an alternative livelihood/rehabilitation package — this is the applicable legal principle.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The reversed-causation trap is in option (c): the inviolate status of CTH is a genuine legal requirement (true), and students may reason backwards that if CTH must be inviolate, relocation must be compulsory. This reverses the actual causal chain — the inviolate status creates an obligation on the State to facilitate voluntary relocation with rehabilitation, not a right to forcibly evict. The Supreme Court has repeatedly upheld this position.
solution.final_explanation:
Critical Tiger Habitats (core zones) under Section 38V of WPA 1972 must be kept inviolate. However, when forest-dwelling communities hold rights under the Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act 2006, these rights cannot be extinguished through forced eviction.

The applicable legal principle is: Relocation from CTH is permissible only if (i) it is voluntary, (ii) the gram sabha passes a resolution consenting to relocation, and (iii) the State provides a comprehensive rehabilitation package before any displacement occurs.

• Option (a) — Correct: The gram sabha must pass a voluntary consent resolution, and rehabilitation must precede physical relocation — this is the FRA 2006 + WPA framework.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Habeas corpus protects against unlawful detention of persons, not land rights violations.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The inviolate status of CTH creates an obligation on the State to negotiate voluntary relocation — it does not authorise forced displacement.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: CAMPA funds support afforestation activities, not the legal process of rights settlement.

Value Addition:
• The Supreme Court's Forest Bench has intervened multiple times on FRA vs. CTH conflicts.
• Gram sabha consent is the constitutionally protected mechanism under the Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act 1996 (PESA) as well.
• As of 2023, several Tiger Reserves still have pending relocation packages — a governance challenge.

solution.concept_anchor: TX2 goal achievement timeline and Global Tiger Day declaration

statement_analysis.statement: The TX2 goal — to double the global wild tiger count from its 2010 baseline — was adopted at the St. Petersburg Tiger Summit in 2010, with a target year of 2022.
statement_analysis.reason: The TX2 (Tiger Times Two) goal was set at the Global Tiger Summit held in St. Petersburg, Russia, in 2010, targeting a doubling of tiger numbers by the Year of the Tiger 2022, from the 2010 baseline.

statement_analysis.statement: India achieved the TX2 goal four years ahead of the 2022 deadline, as evidenced by the 2014 tiger estimation results.
statement_analysis.reason: India achieved the TX2 goal as per the 2018 tiger census (3,167 target had been approached), not the 2014 estimation. The achievement was declared in 2019 at the Global Tiger Day — four years ahead of the 2022 deadline means by 2018, not 2014.

statement_analysis.statement: Global Tiger Day is observed annually on July 29, a date declared at the same St. Petersburg Summit that adopted the TX2 goal.
statement_analysis.reason: Both the TX2 goal and Global Tiger Day (July 29) were declared at the 2010 St. Petersburg Tiger Summit, making this statement correct on both the date and the originating event.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who correctly identify Statements 1 and 3 as true may also accept Statement 2 as true, misrecalling the '4 years ahead' calculation as pointing to 2014 (2022 minus 8 years of 4-year census cycles) rather than 2018.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct: TX2 goal was set at St. Petersburg 2010 summit with 2022 as the target year — this is well-established.

Statement 2 requires precise calculation: '4 years ahead of 2022' means achievement by 2018, not 2014. India's 2018 census showed ~3,000 tigers, and the TX2 achievement was declared in 2019 based on 2018 data — Statement 2 incorrectly names 2014.
Statement 3 is correct: Global Tiger Day (July 29) was indeed declared at the 2010 St. Petersburg Summit.
Statements 1 and 3 correct → option (b): 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap in Statement 2 is precise: '4 years ahead of 2022' should compute to 2018. However, students familiar with the quadrennial census cycle may recall that 2014 was also a census year and could plausibly misassociate the achievement with that year. The correct answer is 2018 — India's PM announced achievement of the TX2 goal at the Global Tiger Day event in 2019 based on 2018 census data.
solution.final_explanation:
The TX2 goal and St. Petersburg Summit together form a critical international conservation milestone that India often cites proudly.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The St. Petersburg Declaration (2010) set the TX2 goal — doubling tiger numbers from the ~3,200 baseline to ~6,400 by 2022 (Year of the Tiger). India's contribution to this goal is the cornerstone of its conservation diplomacy.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: India achieved TX2 ahead of schedule — but '4 years before 2022' means 2018, not 2014. The 2018 tiger census showed ~3,000 tigers (approaching the national TX2 sub-target), and the achievement was formally announced in 2019.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Global Tiger Day (July 29) was declared at the same 2010 St. Petersburg Summit — making it the origin point for both the TX2 goal and the annual awareness day.

Value Addition:
• The Global Tiger Forum is the intergovernmental body coordinating TX2 implementation — India is a founding member, HQ New Delhi.
• 13 tiger range countries signed the St. Petersburg Declaration.
• India's current tiger count (3,167 in 2022) exceeds the global TX2 target of doubling from 2010.

solution.concept_anchor: Countries where tigers are functionally extinct vs. tiger range states
solution.strong_distractor: b — Myanmar is a tiger range state with a declining and threatened population, leading students to incorrectly identify it as functionally extinct alongside Cambodia, Laos, and Vietnam.
elimination_logic: Cambodia, Laos, and Vietnam are countries officially recognised as having functionally extinct wild tiger populations — they share this negative classification.
Myanmar is a recognised tiger range state with documented wild tiger presence, even if the population is critically threatened — it does NOT belong to the 'functionally extinct' category.
The odd one out is Myanmar (option d) — it is a tiger range state with a living population, unlike the other three.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Myanmar is the trap. It borders both Laos and other Southeast Asian nations where tigers are functionally extinct. Myanmar's tiger population is extremely small and threatened, which makes students group it with functionally extinct countries. However, IUCN and tiger range country reports still classify Myanmar as a tiger range state with a documented (if declining) population.
solution.final_explanation:
Among the 13 tiger range countries, some have reached the tragic milestone of functional extinction — where tiger numbers are so low that viable reproduction is no longer occurring in the wild.

• Option (a) Cambodia — Functionally extinct: Wild tigers in Cambodia were declared functionally extinct around 2016; the last confirmed sighting was in the Cardamom Mountains region.
• Option (b) Myanmar — NOT functionally extinct: Myanmar retains documented wild tiger populations, particularly in forested areas near India and Thailand. It is classified as a tiger range state.
• Option (c) Laos — Functionally extinct: Tiger populations in Laos have collapsed; it is widely considered functionally extinct.
• Option (d) Vietnam — Functionally extinct: Vietnam's tiger population is effectively zero in the wild; the last confirmed sighting was over a decade ago.

Myanmar does NOT share the 'functionally extinct' classification → option (b) is the odd one out.

Value Addition:
• All 13 tiger range states signed the St. Petersburg Declaration in 2010.
• CITES Appendix I listing prohibits all commercial international trade in tigers.
• Traditional Chinese Medicine demand for tiger bones and skin remains the primary illegal trade driver.

solution.concept_anchor: Sariska extinction, WPA amendment, Panna reintroduction sequence
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know the WPA was amended in 2006 and Sariska's extinction was confirmed around the same time may place the amendment before the extinction confirmation, reversing the causal sequence.
elimination_logic: Sariska's tiger extinction was confirmed during field surveys in 2004–05 — this is the earliest event.
The Wildlife Protection Act Amendment was enacted in 2006 — directly triggered by the Sariska scandal; this follows the extinction confirmation.
Panna Tiger Reserve lost its last tigers by 2009 — after the WPA amendment but before the reintroduction programme began.
The first tiger reintroduction at Panna began in 2009 (first female tiger introduced) and continued through 2010–11 — the reintroduction programme post-dates all other events.
Correct sequence: Sariska extinction → WPA amendment → Panna extinction → Panna reintroduction → option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap involves Sariska extinction (2004–05) and the WPA amendment (2006). Students who recall '2006' as the key year for both events (NTCA creation + methodology shift) may place the amendment first, assuming it preceded the scandal it was designed to address. The causal chain is the reverse: the scandal caused the amendment. Similarly, conflating Panna's extinction year with its reintroduction year is a one-step reversal trap.
solution.final_explanation:
The Sariska and Panna episodes together form the defining arc of India's tiger conservation crisis and recovery in the 2000s.

Correct sequence:
1. Sariska tiger extinction confirmed (2004–05): Field surveys revealed zero tigers despite pug-mark census data showing a healthy population — the pug-mark method's credibility collapsed.
2. Wildlife Protection Act Amendment enacted (2006): Directly responding to Sariska, Parliament amended WPA to create NTCA and establish a statutory framework for tiger conservation and reserve management.
3. Panna Tiger Reserve loses all tigers (by 2009): The second reserve to suffer complete tiger loss — poor management and poaching; confirmed after the methodology had already shifted.
4. Panna tiger reintroduction programme (2009 onwards): Female tigers sourced from Bandhavgarh and Kanha were introduced; the programme is now considered a success with a recovering population.

Wrong options involve reversing the Sariska-WPA causation or misplacing Panna's extinction vs. reintroduction.

Value Addition:
• Sariska received tigers from Ranthambore for its reintroduction programme.
• Both reintroductions required NTCA approval — no reserve can independently acquire tigers.
• Panna's recovery is often cited as a model for conservation-induced population revival.

solution.concept_anchor: CAMPA fund utility — buffer yes, core no; ESZ vs buffer distinction

statement_analysis.statement: CAMPA funds can be utilised for both core zone and buffer zone management activities within a Tiger Reserve.
statement_analysis.reason: CAMPA funds may be used for buffer zone management but are restricted from core zone activities. Core zones must be kept inviolate, and CAMPA's mandate (compensatory afforestation on degraded land) does not extend to core zone interventions.

statement_analysis.statement: Eco-Sensitive Zones (ESZ) around Tiger Reserves fall within the boundary of the Tiger Reserve and are subject to the same activity restrictions as the buffer zone.
statement_analysis.reason: ESZ lies outside the Tiger Reserve boundary — it is a separate land-use regulation zone notified by MoEFCC under the Environment Protection Act 1986. Buffer zones are inside the Tiger Reserve boundary. They are legally distinct in status, extent, and applicable regulations.

statement_analysis.statement: Tiger Conservation Foundations are state-level bodies mandated by NTCA to raise and manage funds for tiger reserves.
statement_analysis.reason: NTCA mandates that each state with a Tiger Reserve establish a Tiger Conservation Foundation — these are state-level trust bodies designed to mobilise corporate, philanthropic, and other funds for tiger reserve management.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know CAMPA has restrictions may assume both Statements 1 and 2 are incorrect, but Statement 2 specifically about ESZ location is often accepted as correct because ESZs are closely associated with Tiger Reserve governance.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is incorrect: CAMPA funds are available for buffer zone activities but explicitly NOT for core zone activities — the 'both core and buffer' claim makes it wrong.

Statement 2 is incorrect: ESZ lies OUTSIDE the Tiger Reserve boundary (it surrounds the reserve as an outer ring), while the buffer zone lies INSIDE the reserve boundary — confusing the two is a very common error.
Statement 3 is correct: Tiger Conservation Foundations are mandated by NTCA at the state level.
Statements 1 and 2 are NOT correct → option (a): 1 and 2 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in Statement 1 adds 'core zone' to an otherwise partially true statement about CAMPA and buffer zones. Statement 2's trap is the inside/outside confusion regarding ESZ: students who know ESZ surrounds reserves may still think it is part of the reserve's regulatory framework (which it is) and incorrectly conclude it is inside the boundary (which it is not). ESZ = outside boundary; Buffer = inside boundary.
solution.final_explanation:
Tiger reserve finance and spatial zoning are two areas where UPSC has historically tested precision.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: CAMPA (Compensatory Afforestation Fund Management and Planning Authority) funds can support buffer zone development activities, infrastructure in eco-restoration, etc. However, core zones are inviolate — no intervention, including CAMPA-funded activities, is permitted there.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: ESZ is notified by MoEFCC under the Environment Protection Act and lies OUTSIDE the Tiger Reserve's legal boundary. It regulates activities in the surrounding landscape. The buffer zone is INSIDE the Tiger Reserve boundary. This inside/outside distinction is the critical differentiator.
• Statement 3 — Correct: NTCA mandates Tiger Conservation Foundations at the state level. These bodies function as trusts to mobilise CSR funds, donations, and eco-tourism revenues for reserve management beyond government allocations.

Value Addition:
• ESZ activities that are prohibited, regulated, and permitted are defined in individual ESZ notifications — not a uniform blanket ban.
• The Supreme Court's interim order requiring ESZ within 1 km of all protected areas sparked a major controversy in 2022.
• Buffer zones may include reserve forests, community forests, and revenue lands — not all of which are formally Protected Areas under WPA.

solution.concept_anchor: WCCB as statutory body under WPA — not under NTCA
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students associate the WCCB with tiger conservation efforts and therefore pair it with NTCA (which governs tigers), rather than recognising WCCB as an independent statutory body under WPA that operates separately from NTCA.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): Traditional Chinese Medicine demand — bones and skin — is the correct driver; however, verifying that TCM (not food) is the primary demand driver for illegal tiger trade is the key test; this pair might seem correct — verify option (d) before eliminating.

Eliminate option (b): WCCB is a statutory body under WPA but it is NOT under the administrative control of NTCA; it operates independently as the nodal agency for wildlife crime — this pair is incorrectly matched.

Eliminate option (c): CITES Appendix I listing bans commercial international trade — but tigers are listed under Appendix I, not Appendix II (which allows regulated trade); this pair is incorrectly matched.
Confirm option (d): Global Tiger Day on July 29 was declared at the St. Petersburg Tiger Summit 2010 — this is correctly matched.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap in option (b) is the most dangerous: WCCB deals with wildlife crime (including tiger poaching), NTCA governs tiger conservation — both are under WPA and operate in the same domain. Students conflate their institutional relationship, assuming WCCB reports to or is under NTCA. WCCB is an independent statutory body under WPA with its own mandate; it does not fall under NTCA's jurisdiction.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests precision on four distinct tiger conservation facts.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The pair 'tigers : illegal trade driven primarily by food consumption demand' is wrong. The primary demand driver for illegal tiger parts is Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) — particularly bones (for medicine) and skin (for décor). Food consumption is not the primary driver.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: WCCB is described as functioning under NTCA — this is incorrect. The Wildlife Crime Control Bureau is an independent statutory body under the Wildlife Protection Act 1972, functioning under MoEFCC directly. It is the nodal agency for wildlife crime coordination but operates independently of NTCA.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Tigers are listed under CITES Appendix I (strictest protection, commercial trade banned), not Appendix II (regulated trade permitted). This is a status-confusion trap.
• Option (d) — Correct: Global Tiger Day (July 29) was indeed declared at the St. Petersburg Global Tiger Summit in 2010 — the same event that adopted the TX2 goal. This pair is accurately matched.

Value Addition:
• CITES Appendix I = trade ban; Appendix II = regulated trade; Appendix III = one-country protection request.
• Operation Thunderbird is an INTERPOL-coordinated operation targeting bird trafficking; Operation Save Kurma targets turtle/tortoise trafficking — India has participated in both.
• WCCB coordinates with state police, CBI, customs, and INTERPOL for wildlife crime.

solution.concept_anchor: Island biogeography and meta-population management for tigers
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is A correct? A states that small, isolated tiger reserves are more vulnerable to local extinction than large, well-connected ones. This is correct — island biogeography theory applied to habitat fragments shows that small isolated populations face higher extinction risk due to demographic stochasticity, genetic drift, and inbreeding.

Step 2 — Is R correct? R states that WII has developed a meta-population management framework that identifies source and sink tiger populations to manage gene flow through managed translocations. This is correct — WII's framework uses these concepts to recommend translocation between reserves.

Step 3 — Does R causally explain A? R explains the RESPONSE to the vulnerability described in A — it describes a management solution, not the causal mechanism of why isolation leads to extinction risk. The cause of A is island biogeography and genetic bottlenecking, not the absence of WII's framework. R and A are both true but R is a policy response, not the causal explanation of A.
Both A and R are correct, but R does not causally explain A → option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The reversed-causation trap: A describes a biological vulnerability (isolation → extinction risk). R describes a management response (meta-population framework). Students who read R as 'explaining why isolated reserves face extinction' will select option (a). But R actually describes what managers do ABOUT the problem — not why the problem exists. The causal explanation of A lies in island biogeography theory and genetics, not in WII's framework.
solution.final_explanation:
Conservation biology's island biogeography theory underpins modern tiger reserve management — the theory predicts that small, isolated habitat patches behave like islands and lose species over time.

Assertion (A): Isolated small tiger reserves face higher extinction risk than connected large ones — this is correct and grounded in island biogeography (MacArthur-Wilson theory applied to habitat fragments). Demographic stochasticity and inbreeding depression amplify extinction risk in small populations.

Reason (R): WII's meta-population framework classifying reserves as 'source' (exporting tigers) or 'sink' (receiving tigers) to manage gene flow through translocations — this is also factually correct.

Causal relationship: R describes the managerial response to the problem identified in A, not the biological mechanism causing A. The reason isolated reserves are extinction-prone is rooted in population genetics and stochastic demography — not in the presence or absence of a meta-population framework. R and A are both true but causally unconnected.

Answer: option (b) — Both correct, R does NOT explain A.

Value Addition:
• Genetic bottleneck: when a population shrinks severely, it loses allelic diversity, reducing adaptability.
• Sundarbans tiger population is particularly vulnerable to genetic isolation due to its island nature.
• Translocation protocols require NTCA approval, veterinary assessment, and post-release monitoring.

solution.concept_anchor: Special Tiger Reserve geographic facts — size, state, mangrove, UT status

statement_analysis.statement: Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam Tiger Reserve, the largest tiger reserve in India by area, straddles two states.
statement_analysis.reason: Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam is indeed the largest Tiger Reserve in India by area and spans both Andhra Pradesh and Telangana.

statement_analysis.statement: Bor Tiger Reserve in Maharashtra is the smallest Tiger Reserve in India.
statement_analysis.reason: Bor Tiger Reserve in Maharashtra is recognised as the smallest Tiger Reserve in India — it is sometimes confused with Pench, which is also in Maharashtra.

statement_analysis.statement: The Sundarbans Tiger Reserve is the world's only mangrove tiger habitat and is shared between India and Bangladesh as a transboundary reserve under a bilateral treaty.
statement_analysis.reason: Sundarbans is indeed the world's only mangrove tiger habitat and is transboundary (India and Bangladesh), but it is NOT governed by a formal bilateral treaty as a joint 'transboundary reserve' — the Indian and Bangladeshi portions are managed separately under their own national frameworks. 'Shared under a bilateral treaty' overstates the arrangement.

statement_analysis.statement: As of current notification status, no Union Territory of India has a Tiger Reserve.
statement_analysis.reason: All Tiger Reserves in India are located within States, not Union Territories. Andaman & Nicobar Islands (a UT) has no notified Tiger Reserve despite being proposed — this is a common trap question.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who accept all four statements as obviously factual will select 'All four', missing the nuanced incorrectness in Statement 3 about the bilateral treaty claim.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct: Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam spans AP and Telangana — it is the largest Tiger Reserve.
Statement 2 is correct: Bor (Maharashtra) is the smallest Tiger Reserve.

Statement 3 is incorrect: The 'bilateral treaty' element is false — both countries manage their portions separately; there is no formal joint management treaty making it a unified transboundary reserve.
Statement 4 is correct: No UT currently has a Tiger Reserve — Andaman & Nicobar is proposed but not notified.
Three statements correct → option (c): Only three.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The geographic-swap trap in Statement 3 is the scope-extension of 'transboundary with Bangladesh' (true) into 'under a bilateral treaty' (false). Students who know Sundarbans is transboundary will accept the full statement. The critical distinction is that both India and Bangladesh independently manage their portions — there is no formal joint treaty establishing it as a unified transboundary reserve, unlike some international conservation areas.
solution.final_explanation:
Tiger Reserves with special geographic or legal significance are a favourite UPSC topic.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam (~3,728 sq km) is India's largest Tiger Reserve, uniquely straddling Andhra Pradesh and Telangana — a post-state-bifurcation administrative complexity.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Bor Tiger Reserve (~138 sq km) in Vidarbha, Maharashtra, is the smallest. Students must not confuse it with Pench (Maharashtra/MP), which is much larger.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Sundarbans is indeed the world's only mangrove tiger habitat and does straddle India-Bangladesh. However, there is no bilateral treaty creating a jointly managed transboundary reserve — both sides manage their portions (Sundarbans Tiger Reserve, India; Sundarbans National Park, Bangladesh) independently.
• Statement 4 — Correct: All 55+ Tiger Reserves are in States. Andaman & Nicobar Islands (UT) has been proposed for a Tiger Reserve but none is notified.

Three correct → Only three → option (c).

Value Addition:
• Mhadei in Goa is a recently notified Tiger Reserve with inter-state water conflict implications (Karnataka).
• Sundarbans tigers are adapted to swimming — a unique ecological trait not seen in other populations.
• Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam's management coordination between AP and Telangana governments is an ongoing administrative challenge.

solution.concept_anchor: Quadrennial census cycle and 2022 as fifth cycle
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know the census is conducted every four years and that it began in 2006 may miscalculate: 2006, 2010, 2014, 2018, 2022 = 5 cycles. However, some students miscount and assume 2022 is the 4th cycle.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): If the 2022 census were the 4th cycle, the first would have been 2010 — but the census began in 2006, making 2006 the first cycle.

Confirm option (b): Quadrennial (4-year) cycle: 2006 (1st), 2010 (2nd), 2014 (3rd), 2018 (4th), 2022 (5th) — the 2022 census was the 5th cycle.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap is in the cycle numbering. Students who know the census started in 2006 and runs every 4 years may miscalculate '5th' as '4th' or confuse the cycle frequency (thinking it's every 5 years). Counting explicitly: 2006→2010→2014→2018→2022 = five census exercises, each four years apart. The 5th cycle is 2022.
solution.final_explanation:
The All India Tiger Estimation follows a fixed quadrennial schedule since 2006, providing consistent time-series data on tiger population trends.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The 2022 census was the 5th cycle, not the 4th. The 4th cycle was 2018.
• Option (b) — Correct: The census cycle is quadrennial (every 4 years): 2006 (1st), 2010 (2nd), 2014 (3rd), 2018 (4th), 2022 (5th). The 2022 survey covered 20 states and 600+ protected areas.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: A triennial (3-year) cycle would produce different census years and is not the established pattern.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: A 5-year cycle does not match the actual census years.

Value Addition:
• The 6th cycle is expected in 2026.
• The 2022 census involved all four institutional stakeholders: MoEFCC (policy), NTCA (coordination), WII (technical), and State Forest Departments (field surveys).
• States without tigers were still surveyed for negative occupancy data — important for range assessment.

statement_analysis.statement: Under NTCA guidelines, a tiger that has been declared a 'problem animal' due to repeated attacks on humans must be culled immediately to protect local communities.
statement_analysis.reason: NTCA guidelines establish a tiered protocol: a problem tiger is first attempted to be captured and translocated. Culling is the last resort after all non-lethal methods (capture, translocation) are exhausted. Immediate culling without prior attempts at capture is not permitted under the guidelines.

statement_analysis.statement: Sundarbans presents a unique human-tiger conflict context because tigers in this habitat have learned to navigate tidal waterways, bringing them into frequent contact with fishing and honey-collecting communities.
statement_analysis.reason: Sundarbans tigers are unique globally in their adaptation to mangrove and tidal environments. The conflict interface involves fishermen, honey collectors (Mauleys), and wood cutters — all of whom operate deep within mangrove forests — unlike forest-edge conflicts seen elsewhere.

statement_analysis.statement: Compensation for livestock or crop losses caused by tiger attacks is classified as a State subject, with Central Government providing only advisory guidelines rather than mandatory frameworks.
statement_analysis.reason: Under the federal structure, wildlife compensation falls within state jurisdiction. The Central Government (through NTCA) issues guidelines, but the amount, mechanism, and implementation of compensation are determined and funded by state governments. There is no mandatory central compensation framework.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who know NTCA plays a strong role in tiger governance may assume it mandates a central compensation framework, accepting Statement 3 as incorrect and selecting option (d).
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is incorrect: 'Immediate culling' contradicts NTCA's established protocol — capture and translocation must be attempted first; culling is only a last resort.

Statement 2 is correct: Sundarbans' tidal-mangrove context creates a genuinely unique conflict interface — swimming tigers, fishing communities, honey collectors — distinct from standard forest-edge conflicts.
Statement 3 is correct: Compensation for wildlife damage is a State subject; NTCA issues advisory guidelines without mandatory force.
Statements 2 and 3 correct → option (c): 2 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 uses a partial-truth trap: NTCA's 'problem tiger declaration' is a real procedure, but the protocol emphatically does not prescribe immediate culling. Students who know the protocol exists but are fuzzy on the sequencing will accept Statement 1 as true. The actual sequence is: monitoring → tracking → capture attempt → translocation → culling only if all else fails.
solution.final_explanation:
Human-tiger conflict management requires a differentiated approach depending on whether a tiger is 'straying' (temporary, non-aggressive) or a confirmed 'problem tiger' (repeated attacks).

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: NTCA's problem tiger protocol is graduated — immediate culling is not permissible. The sequence is: field assessment and confirmation of problem status → capture/tranquillisation attempt → translocation to a captive facility → culling only as a last resort when all non-lethal options fail. This protocol protects both community safety and the tiger.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Sundarbans is ecologically unique — tigers swim between islands, and communities (fishermen, Mauleys collecting honey, wood cutters) operate within the same tidal landscape. This creates a conflict profile unlike any other tiger habitat in the world.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Wildlife compensation is governed by State policies. Central guidelines (from NTCA/MoEFCC) are advisory. States like Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra have their own compensation rates and disbursement mechanisms.

Value Addition:
• Face masks worn on the back of the head were historically used by Mauleys to deter tiger attacks — tigers prefer ambushing from behind.
• GPS-based rapid response teams are deployed in Sundarbans to manage conflict.
• Straying tigers (found in agricultural areas outside reserves) are typically captured and returned to reserves — not declared problem animals.

solution.concept_anchor: AITE phase structure — occupancy survey is Phase I, not camera traps

statement_analysis.statement: Camera trap deployment is the first phase of the All India Tiger Estimation, after which sign surveys and prey estimation are conducted.
statement_analysis.reason: The AITE follows a phase-wise structure where Phase I is the large-scale sign/occupancy survey (footprints, scrapes, scats), Phase II involves camera trapping in areas where signs are found, followed by prey estimation and habitat assessment. Camera traps are NOT the first phase.

statement_analysis.statement: Habitat quality in the AITE is assessed using Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) data from remote sensing, integrated with field-based ecological surveys.
statement_analysis.reason: The AITE's habitat assessment phase uses Remote Sensing data including NDVI to evaluate vegetation cover and habitat quality, integrated with field surveys. This is a confirmed component of the methodology.

statement_analysis.statement: Tiger density in a given landscape is directly correlated with prey density — reserves with declining ungulate populations are considered at conservation risk irrespective of tiger count.
statement_analysis.reason: The ecological principle of predator-prey correlation is central to AITE's analytical framework. Declining prey density (deer, wild boar, gaur) is a leading indicator of future tiger population decline, even when current tiger numbers appear stable.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students may identify Statement 1 as incorrect (knowing camera traps are not first) but also incorrectly flag Statement 2 as wrong if they haven't specifically studied NDVI usage in AITE.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is incorrect: AITE Phase I = sign/occupancy surveys (not camera traps). Camera trapping follows after sign detection in Phase II.
Statement 2 is correct: NDVI-based remote sensing is an established component of AITE's habitat assessment — not a fabricated detail.
Statement 3 is correct: Predator-prey correlation is foundational to AITE's conservation assessment — prey decline is a leading indicator.
Only Statement 1 is NOT correct → option (a): 1 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in Statement 1 reverses the phase order. Students who know camera traps are central to AITE may assume they are deployed first. The phase structure is crucial: occupancy/sign surveys precede camera deployment, which precedes prey estimation, which precedes habitat assessment. Knowing the existence of each component is less valuable than knowing their sequence.
solution.final_explanation:
The AITE is a structured, multi-phase methodology — not a single camera-trap exercise. Understanding the sequence of phases is critical for exam precision.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: AITE Phase I involves large-scale occupancy surveys — trained field staff record signs of tigers and prey (pugmarks, scats, scrapes, kills) across tiger landscapes. Camera traps are deployed in Phase II in areas where sign surveys indicate tiger presence. The order is sign survey → camera trap → prey estimation → habitat assessment.
• Statement 2 — Correct: NDVI (a measure of vegetation greenness from satellite data) is used in AITE's habitat assessment phase to evaluate forest cover, habitat connectivity, and quality. This is integrated with ground-truthed field data.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The line transect method (distance sampling) estimates ungulate prey density. Tiger density directly follows prey availability — the AITE treats prey collapse as a conservation alert even when current tiger counts look stable.

Value Addition:
• DNA-based fecal analysis (scat DNA) is used to supplement individual ID where camera coverage is sparse.
• NDVI data is sourced from satellites like Landsat and MODIS.
• 'Minimum viable population' — generally considered ~50 breeding individuals — is the threshold below which local extinction risk rises sharply.

solution.concept_anchor: No Tiger Reserve in any Union Territory — Andaman trap
solution.strong_distractor: a — Andaman & Nicobar Islands has been proposed for a Tiger Reserve and has significant wildlife significance — students who know this proposal may incorrectly assume it has been notified.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): Andaman & Nicobar Islands is a Union Territory — any Tiger Reserve proposal there would be unprecedented, and no notification has been issued; this is the classic trap option.
Eliminate option (b): Lakshadweep is a coral island Union Territory with no tiger habitat — entirely implausible as a Tiger Reserve location.
Eliminate option (d): Delhi is a Union Territory but has no viable tiger habitat or any proposed Tiger Reserve.
Confirm option (c): The correct statement is that no Union Territory in India currently has a notified Tiger Reserve — all 55+ reserves are within State jurisdictions.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The plausible-fabrication trap uses Andaman & Nicobar Islands: there have been proposals to explore tiger conservation in the Andamans, and the islands do have significant forest cover and Protected Areas (including a Biosphere Reserve). Students who have read about conservation proposals in Andaman may incorrectly believe a Tiger Reserve exists there. No Tiger Reserve has been notified in any Union Territory as of the latest data.
solution.final_explanation:
Tiger Reserves are notified under Section 38V of the Wildlife Protection Act 1972, on the recommendation of NTCA, by the State Government. This institutional requirement means Union Territories — which are centrally administered — have a different governance pathway for wildlife areas.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Andaman & Nicobar Islands is a UT with extensive forests and Protected Areas, including Saddle Peak National Park and Galathea Biosphere Reserve. However, no Tiger Reserve has been notified here. Proposals have been discussed but not formalised.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Lakshadweep is a coral archipelago — there is no tiger habitat, no forested mainland, and no basis for a Tiger Reserve.
• Option (c) — Correct: No Union Territory of India has a notified Tiger Reserve. All 55+ Tiger Reserves are within States. This is the intended correct answer.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Delhi has no viable tiger habitat and no Tiger Reserve has ever been proposed there.

Value Addition:
• Andaman & Nicobar does have National Parks and a Biosphere Reserve — but these are distinct from Tiger Reserves under WPA.
• Dampa (Mizoram), Manas and Kaziranga (Assam), Namdapha (Arunachal Pradesh) are northeastern Tiger Reserves — all within States, not UTs.
• If a Tiger Reserve is ever proposed in a UT, the Central Government would serve the role analogous to a State Government in the notification process.

solution.concept_anchor: AITE phases — sign survey, DNA analysis, occupancy model, habitat RS
solution.strong_distractor: b — Conflating DNA-based fecal analysis (which involves cameras indirectly) with camera-trap individual ID leads students to pair B with 2 instead of B with 4.
elimination_logic: Large-scale sign surveys covering all tiger landscapes use field staff who record pugmarks, scats, and scrapes — this is Phase I occupancy mapping; A pairs with 3.
DNA-based fecal (scat) analysis provides individual-level identification without cameras — used as a supplementary tool in dense vegetation where camera coverage is sparse; B pairs with 4.
Camera trap 25 sq km grid methodology enables individual tiger identification through stripe pattern photography — this is the core estimation tool of AITE Phase II; C pairs with 1.
Remote sensing using NDVI data provides habitat quality assessment — used in the final phase of AITE; D pairs with 2.
A-3, B-4, C-1, D-2 → option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap mixes DNA analysis (B) with camera trap individual ID (C) — both produce individual-level identification, causing students to conflate them. The key distinction: camera traps identify individuals through stripe patterns visually; DNA fecal analysis identifies individuals through genetic profiling of droppings without any camera involvement. Students must know BOTH tools exist and serve different identification mechanisms.
solution.final_explanation:
The AITE integrates multiple scientific tools across its phases — each serves a distinct analytical purpose.

• A–3 (Landscape-scale sign surveys: Phase I occupancy mapping): Field teams traverse tiger landscapes recording all tiger and prey signs — this produces the occupancy model showing where tigers are present or absent. It determines where camera traps will be deployed in Phase II.
• B–4 (DNA-based fecal analysis: individual ID in dense vegetation without cameras): Scat collected in the field is subjected to genetic analysis. This allows individual tiger identification in areas where camera deployment is difficult — particularly dense forests or river valleys.
• C–1 (Camera trap 25 sq km grid: individual ID via stripe pattern photography): Paired cameras at the same station photograph both flanks of a passing tiger. Since no two tigers share identical stripe patterns, individuals are identified from photographic databases — the core quantitative method of AITE Phase II.
• D–2 (NDVI remote sensing: habitat quality and forest cover assessment): Satellite vegetation indices (NDVI) measure forest cover density and continuity — used in Phase IV habitat assessment to classify landscape quality for tigers.

Value Addition:
• AITE combines all four tools into one integrated national exercise — a methodological first globally.
• Occupancy modelling from Phase I also generates prey distribution maps.
• Camera trap databases are maintained by WII and accessed by all state forest departments.

solution.concept_anchor: Global Tiger Forum headquarters and founding membership

statement_analysis.statement: The Global Tiger Forum is an intergovernmental body dedicated to tiger conservation, with its headquarters located in New Delhi, and India is among its founding members.
statement_analysis.reason: The Global Tiger Forum (GTF) is indeed an intergovernmental organisation with HQ in New Delhi. India is a founding member — GTF was established in 1994 to coordinate tiger conservation among range states.

statement_analysis.statement: CITES places tigers under its Appendix II category, which permits regulated international trade subject to export quotas determined by range countries.
statement_analysis.reason: Tigers are listed under CITES Appendix I — the strictest protection category — which prohibits all commercial international trade. Appendix II allows regulated trade; tigers are not in Appendix II.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know the GTF is real and India is a member may accept Statement 1 while incorrectly accepting Statement 2 (thinking regulated trade is possible for captive tigers, which applies differently under CITES).
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: GTF is headquartered in New Delhi and India is a founding member — this is factually confirmed.
Verify Statement 2: CITES Appendix I = complete commercial trade ban. Appendix II = regulated trade allowed. Tigers are under Appendix I, NOT Appendix II — Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect → option (c): Statement 1 is correct but Statement 2 is incorrect.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap in Statement 2 swaps Appendix I with Appendix II. Students who know tigers are on CITES but are fuzzy on whether it is Appendix I or II — and who know that 'Appendix II allows regulated trade for some species' — may accept Statement 2 as plausible. The distinction is absolute: Appendix I = no commercial trade; Appendix II = permitted with regulation. Tigers have been on Appendix I since 1975.
solution.final_explanation:
International tiger conservation governance involves two distinct frameworks: the Global Tiger Forum (multilateral intergovernmental body) and CITES (trade regulation treaty).

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Global Tiger Forum was established in 1994, bringing together tiger range countries under an intergovernmental framework. Its secretariat is in New Delhi, and India is a founding member. GTF coordinates implementation of the St. Petersburg Declaration and TX2 goal.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: CITES Appendix I covers species threatened with extinction where trade is prohibited for commercial purposes. Tigers have been under Appendix I since 1975. Appendix II covers species where trade is permitted if regulated — tigers are NOT in Appendix II. The error is a classic Appendix I/II swap.

Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect → option (c).

Value Addition:
• CITES was adopted in 1973 and entered into force in 1975 — India is a signatory.
• All 13 tiger range states are members of GTF.
• Appendix III: species protected in at least one country that requests CITES assistance — tigers are not in Appendix III either.

solution.concept_anchor: CTH notified under Section 38V of WPA 1972
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who associate 'Critical Tiger Habitat' with forest rights legislation may incorrectly select the Forest Rights Act 2006 as the source statute, confusing the right to resist displacement (under FRA) with the authority to notify CTH (under WPA).
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (b): Environment Protection Act 1986 is used for ESZ notifications, pollution control, and hazardous substances — not for Tiger Reserve or CTH declarations.
Eliminate option (c): Forest Rights Act 2006 creates rights for forest dwellers within CTH but does NOT provide the authority to declare or notify CTH.
Eliminate option (d): Indian Forest Act 1927 governs reserve forests, protected forests, and forest produce — it has no provision for declaring Tiger Reserves or CTH.
Confirm option (a): Section 38V of the Wildlife Protection Act 1972 is the specific provision under which Critical Tiger Habitats (core zones) are notified — inserted by the 2006 WPA amendment.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap/entity-swap trap conflates the Forest Rights Act 2006 with the WPA 1972 for CTH notifications. Both 2006 Acts deal with the same geographic areas (tiger reserves) and the same communities (tribal forest dwellers). Students studying FRA vs. CTH conflict may incorrectly attribute CTH notification power to FRA. The WPA's Section 38V is the exclusive legal basis for CTH notification.
solution.final_explanation:
Critical Tiger Habitats are the inviolate core zones of Tiger Reserves — legally the most protected land category in India's wildlife framework.

• Option (a) — Correct: Section 38V of the Wildlife Protection Act 1972 (inserted by the 2006 amendment) is the specific provision under which Tiger Reserves, including their core zones (Critical Tiger Habitats), are notified by State Governments on NTCA's recommendation.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The Environment Protection Act 1986 is used for Eco-Sensitive Zone notifications and environmental standards — it has no provision for declaring CTH.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The Forest Rights Act 2006 creates and recognises forest rights of tribal communities within CTH — it does not provide authority to notify or declare CTH. The two Acts operate in tension: WPA creates CTH; FRA protects rights within it.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The Indian Forest Act 1927 governs classification and management of forests (reserved, protected, village forests) — it predates the Tiger Reserve framework by decades.

Value Addition:
• Section 38V requires that CTH be identified based on scientific and objective criteria — species area requirements, ecological sensitivity, and biodiversity richness.
• CTH cannot be de-notified without Central Government approval and State concurrence.
• The 2006 WPA amendment was specifically designed to respond to the Sariska tiger crisis.

solution.concept_anchor: Institutional roles in AITE — MoEFCC, NTCA, WII, State FDs

statement_analysis.statement: The Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change provides overall policy direction for the All India Tiger Estimation.
statement_analysis.reason: MoEFCC is the apex policy body overseeing tiger conservation. The AITE is conducted under its policy framework, with NTCA coordinating implementation.

statement_analysis.statement: The National Tiger Conservation Authority is the statutory body that coordinates the AITE and provides the regulatory framework for Tiger Reserves.
statement_analysis.reason: NTCA's coordination role in AITE is well established — it provides the regulatory and operational mandate under which the census is conducted across states.

statement_analysis.statement: The Wildlife Institute of India serves as the technical partner for the AITE but functions as a statutory body under the Wildlife Protection Act 1972.
statement_analysis.reason: WII is the technical partner for AITE — correct. However, WII is an autonomous institution (not a statutory body) established in 1982 under MoEFCC through an executive resolution, not under WPA.

statement_analysis.statement: State Forest Departments conduct the field surveys (sign surveys and camera trap operations) during the AITE, reporting findings to WII for analysis.
statement_analysis.reason: State Forest Departments are the field implementation arm of AITE — their trained staff conduct occupancy surveys, deploy camera traps, and gather field data, which WII then processes for population estimates.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who know all four entities play legitimate roles in AITE may accept all four statements as correct without detecting the statutory/autonomous distinction for WII.
elimination_logic: Statements 1, 2, and 4 describe MoEFCC, NTCA, and State Forest Departments correctly — their roles are factually established.

Statement 3 contains an entity-swap error: WII is the legitimate technical partner (true), but calling it a 'statutory body under WPA' is false — WII is autonomous, created by executive order, not by WPA.
Three statements correct (1, 2, 4), one incorrect (3) → Only three → option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap in Statement 3 pairs WII (correct entity) with 'statutory body under WPA' (wrong classification). NTCA is the statutory body under WPA; WII is the autonomous research institution. Both operate in tiger conservation, creating a proximity trap. A student who knows WII is important in tiger governance but hasn't specifically memorised 'autonomous institution vs. statutory body' will accept Statement 3 as correct.
solution.final_explanation:
The AITE relies on a four-tier institutional architecture where each body plays a distinct role.

• Statement 1 — Correct: MoEFCC sets the policy framework — it is the parent ministry for both NTCA and WII and provides overall direction for national tiger conservation programmes.
• Statement 2 — Correct: NTCA (statutory body under Chapter IVB of WPA 1972) coordinates the AITE across states, issues notifications, and provides the regulatory framework for tiger reserves.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: WII is indeed the technical partner, conducting surveys and publishing the Status of Tigers report. However, WII is an autonomous institution established in 1982 by executive resolution under MoEFCC — NOT a statutory body under WPA. This distinction is a standard UPSC precision trap.
• Statement 4 — Correct: State Forest Departments are the implementing arm. Their field staff (ranging from frontline guards to wildlife biologists) conduct sign surveys, deploy and retrieve camera traps, and collect data that WII processes centrally.

Three correct → Only three → option (c).

Value Addition:
• The Status of Tigers in India report is co-published by NTCA and WII.
• WII also trains State Forest Department staff in survey methodology.
• WII's Dehradun campus hosts India's only dedicated wildlife research and training infrastructure.
